items.title: India’s Silicon Valley Is Straining Under Its Own Growth
items.content: Bangalore helped turn India into a global hub for software services, tech talent and outsourcing, building an ecosystem that now supports multinational firms, domestic startups and capital. But the city’s success has also become one of its biggest weaknesses. India still lacks the depth of capital available in the US and China, while Bangalore’s physical infrastructure has struggled to keep pace with private-sector growth. At the same time, southern India’s rising economic power is colliding with demographic and political shifts that could threaten its representation in the country’s Central Government, which helps support the growth that cities like Bangalore have enjoyed. (Source: Bloomberg)

items.title: MBA Programs Race to Adapt to the AI Era
items.content: Stanford Graduate School of Business remains atop Bloomberg Businessweek’s US MBA rankings, scoring strongly in areas including compensation, networking and entrepreneurship. Bloomberg Businessweek Senior Editor Dimitra Kessenides is on Bloomberg This Weekend and explains that business schools are also experimenting with AI in teaching, case studies and career preparation as they try to ensure graduates have the skills employers increasingly expect. (Source: Bloomberg)

items.title: A Goldman M&A Banker Helped Bring the Olympics to Los Angeles
items.content: We're in an era of megadeals, with Goldman Sachs reporting a record year for big deal volumes as companies scramble to compete with AI. Gene Sykes has seen multiple deal cycles come and go over his multi-decade career at the firm. The co-head of mergers and acquisitions has worked on famous transactions like Comcast's purchase of Universal and Disney's buyout of Pixar. In addition to being "the most-influential M&A banker you've never heard of," as New York magazine has put it, he has also spearheaded Los Angeles's successful bid to bring the Olympic Games to the city in 2028. In this conversation, recorded live at the Future Proof Festival in Huntington Beach, California, we discuss how a city pays for a big event like the Olympics, and parallels between the early 2000s TMT environment and now. (Source: Bloomberg)

items.title: Clara Wu Tsai on the NY Liberty, Rise of the WNBA | The David Rubenstein Show
items.content: Clara Wu Tsai is one of the most influential sports owners and philanthropists today. In 2019, she and her husband, Joe Tsai, bought the New York Liberty, where she helped transform the franchise into a WNBA championship team by investing in players, facilities, management and the fan experience. Wu Tsai, who also co-owns the Brooklyn Nets, explains why sports have become a legitimate asset class and why live sports are increasingly valuable in the age of AI. She also reflects on her journey from growing up in Kansas as the daughter of immigrants from Taiwan, to building a career in business as well as her philanthropy, and the lessons she's learned about leadership, opportunity and success. Wu Tsai joins David Rubenstein for the premiere episode of The David Rubenstein Show: Peer to Peer Conversations, Season 12. This interview was recorded June 4, in Brooklyn, New York.  (Source: Bloomberg)

She speaks with Romaine Bostick & Jess Menton on "The Close." (Source: Bloomberg)

items.title: Investing for the AI Boom: Masters in Business with Glen Kacher
items.content: Barry speaks with Glen Kacher, Managing Director and CIO of Light Street Capital. They discuss his tenure at Integral Capital Partners, as well as his start at Tiger Management under founder Julian Robertson. They discuss being a hedge fund surrounded by venture capital in Silicon Valley, as well as learning to embrace the speed of tech. They also discuss the polarization of data centers and what AI will look like five years from now. (Source: Bloomberg)

items.title: Crusoe CEO: Data Center Indusry Has a 'Marketing Issue’
items.content: Crusoe CEO Chase Lochmiller discusses the AI infrastructure company's nearly $4 billion in fresh funding sending its valuation to almost $31 billion. He also discusses how it will fuel the company’s push to build AI infrastructure spanning data centers, cloud computing and managed AI services. He says Crusoe could eventually enter the public markets and pushes back against growing opposition to data centers, arguing the industry has a “marketing issue” and needs to better communicate its impact on water, jobs and local tax revenue. He joins Ed Ludlow on "Bloomberg Tech." (Source: Bloomberg)
